clinicalPearls: A rare, highly aggressive systemic proliferation of natural killer cells, strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus
More prevalent in East Asian and some other populations and tends to affect younger to middle-aged adults
Presents with a fulminant course of fever, hepatosplenomegaly and rapidly progressive cytopenias
Frequently complicated by disseminated intravascular coagulation and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
Circulating and marrow NK cells show an aberrant immunophenotype and clonal EBV
Distinguished from chronic NK-cell lymphoproliferative disorders by its aggressive, often fatal behaviour
It overlaps biologically with extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma of nasal type
reference.pathophysiology: Aggressive NK-cell leukaemia is a clonal, EBV-driven malignancy of natural killer cells. Latent EBV infection within the neoplastic cells contributes to their survival and proliferation, and the cells release inflammatory cytokines that drive systemic features and can trigger haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Widespread infiltration of blood, bone marrow, liver and spleen produces profound cytopenias, organ dysfunction and coagulopathy, accounting for the fulminant, rapidly fatal clinical course.
additionalDifferentials: Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type, in leukaemic phase
Chronic lymphoproliferative disorder of NK cells
Reactive NK-cell expansion with EBV infection
additionalInvestigations: Blood film and flow cytometry demonstrating an aberrant NK-cell population
EBV studies including EBV-encoded RNA on tissue and viral load
Assessment for haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and coagulation status
Imaging to evaluate hepatosplenomegaly and organ involvement
redFlags: Fulminant illness with high fever and rapidly falling blood counts
reference.prognosis: Aggressive NK-cell leukaemia has a very poor prognosis with short survival despite intensive therapy; asparaginase-containing regimens and allogeneic stem cell transplantation offer the only realistic prospect of prolonged remission in selected patients.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for a reactive EBV-driven process or benign NK-cell expansion
Attributing cytopenias and fever solely to infection and delaying diagnosis
Using standard regimens without asparaginase, which are typically ineffective
management: Initiate intensive asparaginase-containing chemotherapy promptly, as anthracycline-based regimens are typically ineffective against this multidrug-resistant malignancy
Consolidate responding, fit patients with allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, the only realistic route to durable remission
Recognise and treat associated haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis urgently with immunochemotherapy and organ support
Manage disseminated intravascular coagulation with blood product support including fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate and platelets
Provide intensive supportive care with transfusion, tumour lysis prophylaxis and prevention and treatment of opportunistic infection
Refer urgently to a transplant-capable haemato-oncology centre and involve palliative care given the poor prognosis
